tracks.legalName: Automatic deletion of traffic offense records, Utah Code 77-40a-202
tracks.publicName: Utah deletes old traffic cases automatically

controllingAuthority.summary: The court deletes traffic offense records on its own initiative. A traffic offense means an infraction or class B or C misdemeanour under Title 41 Chapter 6a, Title 53 Chapter 3 Part 2 and Title 73 Chapter 18, plus substantially similar local ordinances. Title 41 Chapter 6a Part 5, driving under the influence and reckless driving, and Sections 73-18-13 through 73-18-13.6 are expressly not traffic offenses, so DUI is not a traffic offense in Utah. Deletion follows an acquittal on all charges, a dismissal with prejudice other than one resulting from successful completion of a plea in abeyance, or adjudication plus five years for class C misdemeanours and infractions or six years for class B misdemeanours. Where the qualifying event occurred on or after 2020-05-01 the court deletes on identification; where it occurred before that date the court deletes within one year of identification. The court deletes and BCI neither receives nor indexes expunged traffic offenses, so traffic expungement enquiries go to the court rather than to BCI. The duty is mandatory.

exclusions: Driving under the influence and reckless driving under Title 41 Chapter 6a Part 5, and the boating equivalents at Sections 73-18-13 through 73-18-13.6, together with substantially similar local ordinances. DUI is not a traffic offense in Utah.
A dismissal with prejudice resulting from successful completion of a plea in abeyance.
Offences above class B misdemeanour, which fall outside the traffic offense definition entirely.
This track offers no participant filing. Where the participant cannot wait for the automatic deletion, the paid alternative is the UT-PET-07 traffic conviction petition.

tracks.legalName: Automatic expungement after acquittal or dismissal with prejudice, Utah Code 77-40a-206
tracks.publicName: Utah clears acquittals and dismissals automatically

controllingAuthority.summary: Where a person is acquitted on all charges the court expunges the case 60 days after the acquittal. Where the case is dismissed with prejudice the court expunges 180 days after the day of dismissal if no appeal was filed, or after a final non-appealable order if one was. A case dismissed with prejudice as a result of successful completion of a plea in abeyance agreement is excluded, as is a case in which the person was found not guilty by reason of insanity. Since 2026-01-01 the identification duty at 77-40a-204(3) puts the work on the court's own initiative and form 1200EX is retired. The duty is mandatory once the case is identified. Section 77-40a-204 does not preclude filing a petition for a case that is eligible for automatic expungement where the automatic expungement has not occurred, which is what makes the petition tracks a genuine fallback rather than a duplicate.

exclusions: A case dismissed with prejudice as a result of successful completion of a plea in abeyance agreement.
A case in which the person was found not guilty by reason of insanity.

This track offers no participant filing. Where the automatic expungement has not occurred, the fallback is the UT-PET-02 or UT-PET-04 petition.

tracks.publicName: Utah's Clean Slate: some convictions clear themselves

controllingAuthority.summary: Every conviction in the case must be a misdemeanour for possession of a controlled substance under Subsection 58-37-8(2)(a)(i), a class B misdemeanour, a class C misdemeanour, or an infraction. The waiting periods run from the day the individual is adjudicated: five years for class C misdemeanours and infractions, six years for class B misdemeanours, and seven years for class A misdemeanour possession of a controlled substance under 58-37-8(2)(a)(i). The prosecuting agency receives notice and may object; if 35 days pass without a written objection the court proceeds. Since 2026-01-01 the court identifies eligible cases on its own initiative under 77-40a-204(3), and form 1200EX is retired. For cases adjudicated on or after 2020-05-01 that are not traffic offenses the target is expungement within 30 days of the court determining requirements are satisfied; for cases adjudicated or dismissed before that date, within one year of identification. In practice the process can take up to 120 days because the court runs the job monthly and must allow the objection window.

exclusions: A pending misdemeanour or felony proceeding.
Incarceration, probation or parole as of 2025-01-01 for an individual seeking automatic expungement on and after that date.
A not-guilty-by-reason-of-insanity finding.
Unsatisfied state debt, or a criminal accounts receivable entered as a civil judgment and transferred to the Office of State Debt Collection.
Conviction counts exceeding the 77-40a-303(4) or (5) limits.

Any plea in abeyance or conviction for a felony; a class A misdemeanour other than drug possession; a capital felony; a first degree felony; a violent felony under 76-3-203.5(1)(c)(i); felony DUI; a registerable sex offence; a registerable child abuse offence; an offence against a person under Title 76 Chapter 5; a weapons offence under Title 76 Chapter 10 Part 5; sexual battery; lewdness; DUI or reckless driving; damage to or interruption of a communication device; or domestic violence.
This track offers no participant filing. Where the case is not eligible, or the wait has not run, the paid petition tracks are the alternative.

rules.filing: Filed in the court that decided the case, district or justice court, under Utah Code 77-40a-305. The packet is the civil cover sheet, the petition, the proposed order and the BCI certificate of eligibility, with the filing fee or a fee waiver request. The certificate must still be valid on the filing date. Certified copies of a granted order must be requested within 28 days after the order is granted (URCrP 42).
rules.fees: A court filing fee set by Utah Code 78A-2-301 applies. The Utah Courts page directs filers to the cover sheet for the current amount rather than publishing a figure, so the packet does not quote one. The exact current amount is an open release-blocking question.
rules.feeWaiver: The court fee waiver process applies to the filing fee, and the published packet includes the fee waiver route. BCI separately operates an indigency-linked waiver and will issue without the issuance fee where the court is likely to waive the filing fee; if the court then finds the petitioner not indigent, the BCI issuance fee must be paid before BCI will process the expungement order.
rules.notice: The court sends a copy of the filing to the prosecuting attorney. The prosecutor has 35 days to file an objection or statement, including on a victim's behalf; the victim has 60 days. The court must wait 60 days from filing before acting. The petitioner may reply to a prosecutor or victim statement within 14 days of receiving it. The court may order Adult Probation and Parole to file a written response, which AP&P serves on the petitioner, the prosecutor and the victim, and to which the petitioner may reply within 14 days.
rules.service: The petitioner does not effect service in the ordinary case: the court sends the filing to the prosecuting attorney. The Proof of Service form appears in the published packet only as an optional form, used where the prosecutor's office will not accept service. The Utah Courts general service-of-process page governs first papers in a new civil case and must not be wired to this track; doing so would import a summons, a process server and a 120-day deadline this track does not have.
rules.participantSignature: The petitioner signs the petition. The proposed order is completed by the petitioner except for the judge's signature line, which is left blank. The Consent and Waiver of Hearing is presented by the petitioner and signed by the prosecuting attorney; LegalEase neither obtains that consent nor signs on anyone's behalf.
rules.notarization: Not required by Chapter 40a or by the published Utah Courts expungement packet for the petition itself.

legalDesignDecision.rationale: Approved as a two-stage packet-capable track. Venue is the district court in the county of arrest rather than the deciding court, because no case exists — that is the one venue variation in Utah and it is recorded explicitly. The final-decision-not-to-file fact is asked as a participant question with an evidence prompt rather than asserted, since it is frequently undocumented; BCI's certificate decision is the operative check. The route is composed as a sequential composition because the two stages are legally distinct in every way the schema asks about: a different actor decides each one, they go to different destinations, the participant makes a different submission at each, they have different legal effects — an administrative certificate of eligibility, then a judicial order of expungement — and the sequence is a legal condition rather than a convenience, because 77-40a-305 requires the certificate and 77-40a-306(1) requires it to be valid at filing. It is not composition for record-gathering or for ordinary post-filing handoff: LegalEase generates the BCI application itself, as a participant-facing agency submission, rather than telling the participant to go and fetch a record. Both units are official_pdf_fill because both stages have current official participant-facing forms and LegalEase completes only the participant portions, leaving the judge's signature, the prosecutor's consent and BCI's determination blank. Nothing here is withheld because an outside party must later act: the BCI determination, the prosecutor's consent, the victim window, the discretionary hearing and the judge's signature are all recorded as prerequisites, manual completion items or handoffs, not as generation blockers.

limitations.statement: Eligibility is determined by BCI, not by LegalEase. The review classifies any in-product eligibility opinion for conviction cases as a legal-design blocker. That is honoured by restricting the track rather than by asserting an opinion: LegalEase routes to BCI, prepares the stage-one application, and treats the certificate as the eligibility answer. No element of the design is undetermined, so this is a scope restriction rather than a build blocker.

legalDesignDecision.rationale: Approved as a two-stage packet-capable track, with the free automatic alternative disclosed before payment. The plea-in-abeyance question is asked because a case that has not actually been dismissed is not on this track at all and needs a Motion to Dismiss first; that prerequisite is recorded as a packet instruction and a stop condition rather than folded into the expungement packet, because it is a different filing under the general motions forms. The route is composed as a sequential composition because the two stages are legally distinct in every way the schema asks about: a different actor decides each one, they go to different destinations, the participant makes a different submission at each, they have different legal effects — an administrative certificate of eligibility, then a judicial order of expungement — and the sequence is a legal condition rather than a convenience, because 77-40a-305 requires the certificate and 77-40a-306(1) requires it to be valid at filing. It is not composition for record-gathering or for ordinary post-filing handoff: LegalEase generates the BCI application itself, as a participant-facing agency submission, rather than telling the participant to go and fetch a record. Both units are official_pdf_fill because both stages have current official participant-facing forms and LegalEase completes only the participant portions, leaving the judge's signature, the prosecutor's consent and BCI's determination blank. Nothing here is withheld because an outside party must later act: the BCI determination, the prosecutor's consent, the victim window, the discretionary hearing and the judge's signature are all recorded as prerequisites, manual completion items or handoffs, not as generation blockers.

rules.filing: Filed in the court that decided the case, district or justice court, under Utah Code 77-40a-305. The packet is the civil cover sheet, the petition, the proposed order and the BCI certificate of eligibility, with the filing fee or a fee waiver request. The certificate must still be valid on the filing date. Certified copies of a granted order must be requested within 28 days after the order is granted (URCrP 42).
rules.fees: A court filing fee set by Utah Code 78A-2-301 applies. The Utah Courts page directs filers to the cover sheet for the current amount rather than publishing a figure, so the packet does not quote one. The exact current amount is an open release-blocking question.
rules.feeWaiver: The court fee waiver process applies to the filing fee, and the published packet includes the fee waiver route. BCI separately operates an indigency-linked waiver and will issue without the issuance fee where the court is likely to waive the filing fee; if the court then finds the petitioner not indigent, the BCI issuance fee must be paid before BCI will process the expungement order.
rules.notice: The court sends a copy of the filing to the prosecuting attorney. The prosecutor has 35 days to file an objection or statement, including on a victim's behalf; the victim has 60 days. The court must wait 60 days from filing before acting. The petitioner may reply to a prosecutor or victim statement within 14 days of receiving it. The court may order Adult Probation and Parole to file a written response, which AP&P serves on the petitioner, the prosecutor and the victim, and to which the petitioner may reply within 14 days.
rules.service: The petitioner does not effect service in the ordinary case: the court sends the filing to the prosecuting attorney. The Proof of Service form appears in the published packet only as an optional form, used where the prosecutor's office will not accept service. The Utah Courts general service-of-process page governs first papers in a new civil case and must not be wired to this track; doing so would import a summons, a process server and a 120-day deadline this track does not have.
rules.participantSignature: The petitioner signs the petition. The proposed order is completed by the petitioner except for the judge's signature line, which is left blank. The Consent and Waiver of Hearing is presented by the petitioner and signed by the prosecuting attorney; LegalEase neither obtains that consent nor signs on anyone's behalf.
rules.notarization: Not required by Chapter 40a or by the published Utah Courts expungement packet for the petition itself.

rules.filing: Filed in the court that decided the case, district or justice court, under Utah Code 77-40a-305. The packet is the civil cover sheet, the petition, the proposed order and the BCI certificate of eligibility, with the filing fee or a fee waiver request. The certificate must still be valid on the filing date. Certified copies of a granted order must be requested within 28 days after the order is granted (URCrP 42).
rules.fees: A court filing fee set by Utah Code 78A-2-301 applies. The Utah Courts page directs filers to the cover sheet for the current amount rather than publishing a figure, so the packet does not quote one. The exact current amount is an open release-blocking question.
rules.feeWaiver: The court fee waiver process applies to the filing fee, and the published packet includes the fee waiver route. BCI separately operates an indigency-linked waiver and will issue without the issuance fee where the court is likely to waive the filing fee; if the court then finds the petitioner not indigent, the BCI issuance fee must be paid before BCI will process the expungement order.
rules.notice: The court sends a copy of the filing to the prosecuting attorney. The prosecutor has 35 days to file an objection or statement, including on a victim's behalf; the victim has 60 days. The court must wait 60 days from filing before acting. The petitioner may reply to a prosecutor or victim statement within 14 days of receiving it. The court may order Adult Probation and Parole to file a written response, which AP&P serves on the petitioner, the prosecutor and the victim, and to which the petitioner may reply within 14 days.
rules.service: The petitioner does not effect service in the ordinary case: the court sends the filing to the prosecuting attorney. The Proof of Service form appears in the published packet only as an optional form, used where the prosecutor's office will not accept service. The Utah Courts general service-of-process page governs first papers in a new civil case and must not be wired to this track; doing so would import a summons, a process server and a 120-day deadline this track does not have.
rules.participantSignature: The petitioner signs the petition. The proposed order is completed by the petitioner except for the judge's signature line, which is left blank. The Consent and Waiver of Hearing is presented by the petitioner and signed by the prosecuting attorney; LegalEase neither obtains that consent nor signs on anyone's behalf.
rules.notarization: Not required by Chapter 40a or by the published Utah Courts expungement packet for the petition itself.

legalDesignDecision.rationale: Approved as a two-stage packet-capable track. The distinguishing design decision is that the limitations computation is deliberately not performed in product: the certificate stage applies the screen, and BCI's refusal is the answer. That is a scope restriction on what LegalEase asserts, not an undetermined element — the mechanism, vehicle, court, venue, contents and geographic scope are all settled, so nothing is withheld. The route is composed as a sequential composition because the two stages are legally distinct in every way the schema asks about: a different actor decides each one, they go to different destinations, the participant makes a different submission at each, they have different legal effects — an administrative certificate of eligibility, then a judicial order of expungement — and the sequence is a legal condition rather than a convenience, because 77-40a-305 requires the certificate and 77-40a-306(1) requires it to be valid at filing. It is not composition for record-gathering or for ordinary post-filing handoff: LegalEase generates the BCI application itself, as a participant-facing agency submission, rather than telling the participant to go and fetch a record. Both units are official_pdf_fill because both stages have current official participant-facing forms and LegalEase completes only the participant portions, leaving the judge's signature, the prosecutor's consent and BCI's determination blank. Nothing here is withheld because an outside party must later act: the BCI determination, the prosecutor's consent, the victim window, the discretionary hearing and the judge's signature are all recorded as prerequisites, manual completion items or handoffs, not as generation blockers.

tracks.legalName: Expungement of a conviction on a certificate of eligibility, Utah Code 77-40a-303

controllingAuthority.summary: A conviction may be expunged on petition where all fines and interest are paid in full, all restitution is paid in full, and the applicable waiting period has elapsed, counted from the date the case finished, release from incarceration, or the end of probation or parole, whichever is most recent. The periods are ten years for a misdemeanour under 41-6a-501(2) and a felony under 58-37-8(2)(g); seven years for a felony; five years for a class A misdemeanour and for felony drug possession; four years for a class B misdemeanour; and three years for any other misdemeanour or infraction. Capital felonies, first degree felonies, violent felonies under 76-3-203.5(1)(c)(i), felony automobile homicide, felony DUI under 41-6a-501(2), registerable sex offences under 77-41-102 and registerable child abuse offences under 77-43-102(2) are permanently ineligible. The conviction-count bars at 77-40a-303(4) and (5) are measured against the entire criminal history including previously expunged and out-of-state convictions, with a separate allowance of up to four drug possession offences and a mixed-episode counting rule at 77-40a-303(6). Relief is discretionary in the sense that the court must find by clear and convincing evidence that expungement is not contrary to the public interest, and the petition form itself asks the petitioner to explain why.

exclusions: Capital felony; first degree felony; a felony conviction of a violent felony as defined in Subsection 76-3-203.5(1)(c)(i); a felony conviction described in Subsection 41-6a-501(2); and an offence, or a combination of offences, requiring registration as a sex offender, kidnap offender or child abuse offender under Title 53, Chapter 29, at the time of sentencing or at the time of the application for the certificate. Read at source on 2026-08-06. The controlling review listed felony automobile homicide as a separate permanent bar; the current statute does not, and that item is corrected out here rather than carried. The review's registry citations to 77-41-102 and 77-43-102(2) are likewise superseded by Title 53, Chapter 29.

The 77-40a-303(2)(a) bars do not apply to a conviction for a qualifying sexual offence as defined in Section 76-3-209 committed at age 14 through 17, unless the petitioner was convicted by a district court as an adult under Title 80, Chapter 6, Part 5.

rules.filing: Filed in the court that decided the case, district or justice court, under Utah Code 77-40a-305. legalDesignDecision.rationale: Approved as a two-stage packet-capable track with a mandatory attorney-review offer before filing. This is a separate track rather than a variant of the ordinary certificate route because it uses a different petition and a different order — 1001EX and 1021EX rather than 1000EX and 1020EX — and because the eligibility decision moves from BCI to the court, shifting the evidentiary burden to the petitioner. The review's phrase official_pdf_fill plus mandatory attorney review is normalised as an official_pdf_fill stage-two unit with the attorney review recorded as a post_generation_handoff and a self-help boundary: the packet still generates, because the mechanism, forms, court, venue and contents are all known, and the handoff attaches to an actual event — a contested evidentiary showing before the court. controllingAuthority.summary: Sections 77-40a-305 and 77-40a-306(1) allow a petition for a conviction related to cannabis possession without a certificate of eligibility, where the petition makes the required showing. The petitioner must show a qualifying condition at the time of the arrest or citation; that the cannabis was in a form allowed by law, meaning tablet, capsule, concentrated liquid or viscous oil, liquid suspension, topical, transdermal, sublingual, gelatinous cube or lozenge, resin or wax, or unprocessed flower in a compliant container, or a form measured in grams, milligrams or millilitres; and that the amount did not exceed the medicinal amount, up to 113 grams by weight of unprocessed cannabis in a medicinal dosage form, or 20 grams of total composite tetrahydrocannabinol in a cannabis product in medicinal dosage form. The citation question the controlling review left open is resolved: section 77-40a-305(4)(a), read at its official locator on 2026-08-06, itself cites Section 26B-4-201, which defines a qualifying condition by reference to Section 26B-4-203 where the conditions are listed. Title 26 Chapter 61a, which Utah Courts materials still cite, publishes no current version on the Legislature's site. The packet is cover sheet 1044XX, petition 1003EX, order 1023EX, and the 1146XX and 1148XX forms.

tracks.legalName: Motion to remove the link between personal identifying information and a dismissed criminal case, Utah Code 77-40a-105
tracks.publicName: Break the link between your name and a dismissed case

controllingAuthority.summary: Read at source on 2026-08-06. An individual whose criminal case is dismissed may move the court for an order removing the link between the individual's personal identifying information and the dismissed case in any publicly searchable database of the Utah state courts. Personal identifying information means a current name, former name, nickname or alias, together with date of birth. The court shall grant the motion if 30 days have passed from the day the case was dismissed, no appeal was filed within that 30-day period, and no charge in the case was a domestic violence offence as defined in Section 77-36-1. Relief is ministerial rather than discretionary once those three conditions are met. Two express limits define what the remedy is worth: under subsection (3) removing the link does not affect a prosecuting, arresting or other agency's records, and under subsection (4) the case history, unless expunged under the chapter, remains public and accessible through a search by case number. The remedy therefore breaks the name-to-case search path in the state courts' public database and does nothing else. The companion provision at Utah Code 78B-7-1002.1 gives the same relief to a person against whom a civil protective order or civil stalking injunction was sought and denied; that branch is a civil matter outside the record-clearing product scope and is not built here.

exclusions: Any case in which a charge was a domestic violence offence as defined in Section 77-36-1. This is an absolute bar under 77-40a-105(2)(b)(iii).
Any case dismissed fewer than 30 days ago.
Any case in which an appeal was filed within the 30-day period following dismissal.

A denied request for a civil protective order or a civil stalking injunction. That branch is governed by Utah Code 78B-7-1002.1, is a civil matter, and is outside the record-clearing product scope even though the same form covers it.
Agency records. Subsection (3) is explicit that removing the link does not affect a prosecuting, arresting or other agency's records, so this track is not a substitute for expungement.
An unfinished case. Nothing is available on any petition track while the case is still open.
Unpaid fines, fees, restitution or interest on the case.
A pending criminal case other than a traffic case.
Current incarceration, probation or parole.
A civil protective order, a criminal protective order or a criminal stalking injunction against the petitioner that is in effect, whether or not it relates to the case being cleared.

waitingPeriods.duration: At least 30 days from the day on which the case was dismissed.
No appeal may have been filed in the dismissed case within that same 30-day period.
This remedy runs on a 30-day clock, against the 180 days a dismissal with prejudice waits for automatic expungement under 77-40a-206. It is the faster interim step, not a replacement.

tracks.legalName: Appellate record expungement, Utah Supreme Court Standing Order No. 12

citations: Utah Supreme Court Standing Order No. 12
controllingAuthority.summary: Standing Order No. 12 governs expungement of appellate court records. The prerequisite is an existing district court order expunging the entire trial court record and the records held by other government entities. What is filed with the Utah Supreme Court, and served on the Utah Attorney General, is a written petition, a copy of the district court expungement petition, a certified copy of the district court expungement order, and a proposed redacted appellate opinion replacing the petitioner's name with initials or a pseudonym and redacting address, birthdate and government identification numbers. The Attorney General has 30 days from service to object to the expungement or to the proposed redaction. If granted, appellate records including briefs are sealed, the published opinion is replaced with the redacted version, and the appellate courts notify LexisNexis and Westlaw; other publishers are not legally required to redact. Utah Courts states expressly that there are no forms for this.

exclusions: Any case where the district court has not already expunged the entire trial court record and the records held by other government entities. That order is a prerequisite, not a step on this track.

tracks.publicName: Not eligible yet? Reducing the conviction level may open a route

controllingAuthority.summary: This node produces no record-clearing relief and no packet of its own. A motion to reduce a conviction, commonly called a 402 motion, is not a record-clearing mechanism, but Utah Courts routes ineligible petitioners to it and a reduction can convert an ineligible conviction into an eligible one by changing the offence level and therefore both the applicable waiting period and the conviction-counting math under 77-40a-303 and 77-40a-205. The adopted counsel structure places it in the Utah decision tree as an adjacent non-relief routing node — a not yet, but here is the path branch — and expressly not as a relief track.

exclusions: This node offers no record-clearing relief and generates no packet. It screens and routes.
The reduction motion itself is a sentencing remedy under Title 76 and is outside the record-clearing product scope. It is named here, not built here.

waitingPeriods.duration: A reduction changes the offence level, which changes the applicable expungement waiting period — ten, seven, five, four or three years under 77-40a-303 — and the conviction-counting math. The node exists to name that path where the participant is not eligible today.

geography.venue: Not applicable. This node screens and routes; it has no venue of its own. A reduction motion, if pursued, is filed in the court that entered the conviction.

destination.name: None of its own — the court that entered the conviction, for the reduction motion this node names
destination.detail: Nothing is submitted on this node. It explains why the participant is not eligible for expungement today, identifies whether a reduction in the offence level would change that, and either routes back into an expungement track once the conviction level and the waiting period line up, or refers the participant out for the reduction motion, which is a sentencing remedy outside this product.

components.notes: Routing and expectation-setting. Establishes which bar the participant actually hit — waiting period not yet run, offence level too high, or conviction count over the limit; explains that a reduction under 76-3-402 changes the offence level and therefore both the waiting period and the counting math; states plainly that LegalEase does not prepare the reduction motion and that it is a separate sentencing remedy; and sets the return path, which is to re-run the expungement screen once a reduction has been granted. Where the bar was the conviction count rather than the level, it says so, because a reduction may not help.
